topic.subject: science
topic.title: Fun with magnets
topic.scope: magnetic and non-magnetic materials, poles, attraction and repulsion, compass, storing magnets

misconceptions.statement: All metals are attracted to magnets.
misconceptions.why: Students observe iron objects being attracted and generalize this property to all shiny metallic objects.
misconceptions.fix: Only specific metals like iron, nickel, and cobalt are magnetic; others like aluminum, copper, and gold are not.

probe.question: Will a magnet pick up an aluminum soda can or a copper wire?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they are both metals.

misconceptions.root_belief: all members of a category share one property

misconceptions.statement: If you break a magnet in half, you get one North pole piece and one South pole piece.
misconceptions.why: Intuition suggests that if a whole has two ends, cutting it separates those ends into independent parts.
misconceptions.fix: Breaking a magnet creates two smaller magnets, each with its own North and South pole.

probe.question: If you break a bar magnet in the middle, what poles will the two new pieces have?
probe.wrong_answer: One piece will be only North and the other only South.

misconceptions.root_belief: parts of a whole are independent units
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: The center of a bar magnet is the strongest part.
misconceptions.why: Students often believe the center of an object is its most important or powerful point.
misconceptions.fix: The magnetic strength is maximum at the poles (ends) and minimum at the center.

probe.question: Where will a bar magnet pick up the most iron filings?
probe.wrong_answer: In the middle of the bar.

misconceptions.root_belief: center is the most important part

misconceptions.statement: If an object is attracted to a magnet, it must be a magnet itself.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the property of being magnetic (material) with being a magnet (source).
misconceptions.fix: Magnetic materials like iron are attracted to magnets, but only another magnet can be repelled.

probe.question: An iron nail is pulled toward a magnet. Does this prove the nail is a magnet?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because attraction only happens between two magnets.

misconceptions.statement: A compass needle points North because it is attracted to the North Star.
misconceptions.why: Students associate the word 'North' with the most famous northern celestial object they know.
misconceptions.fix: A compass needle aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, which acts like a giant hidden magnet.

probe.question: Why does a compass needle point North even during the day when stars aren't visible?
probe.wrong_answer: It can still feel the pull of the North Star through the sky.

misconceptions.root_belief: visible or famous objects cause effects

misconceptions.statement: Magnets work like glue or sticky tape.
misconceptions.why: Students use everyday experiences with adhesives to explain non-contact forces.
misconceptions.fix: Magnetism is a force that acts even without touching; it is not a physical sticky substance.

probe.question: Can a magnet attract a pin through a thin piece of paper?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the 'stickiness' cannot go through the paper.

misconceptions.root_belief: forces require physical contact to work

misconceptions.statement: A large magnet will always attract a small magnet, even if like poles are facing.
misconceptions.why: The belief that size or strength overrides the fundamental rules of magnetic poles.
misconceptions.fix: No matter the size, like poles will always repel each other.

probe.question: What happens if you push the North pole of a huge magnet toward the North pole of a tiny magnet?
probe.wrong_answer: The big one will pull the small one because it is stronger.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: A magnet's power gets used up over time like a battery.
misconceptions.why: Analogy with other portable sources of 'power' or 'energy' that deplete with use.
misconceptions.fix: A magnet does not lose its strength by being used; it only loses it if heated, dropped, or hammered.

probe.question: If I use a magnet to pick up 100 pins every day, will it eventually stop working?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will run out of magnetism.

misconceptions.statement: Only iron is magnetic; other metals like nickel are not.
misconceptions.why: Iron is the most common magnetic material mentioned in textbooks and daily life.
misconceptions.fix: While iron is common, nickel and cobalt are also naturally magnetic metals.

probe.question: Which of these is magnetic: Iron, Nickel, or both?

misconceptions.root_belief: one example represents the whole class

misconceptions.statement: Heating a magnet makes it stronger because it gives it more energy.
misconceptions.why: Generalization that adding heat energy always increases the 'power' of a physical property.
misconceptions.fix: Heating a magnet actually destroys its magnetic alignment, making it lose its magnetism.

probe.question: What happens to a magnet if you heat it strongly over a flame?
probe.wrong_answer: It becomes a much stronger magnet.

misconceptions.root_belief: more energy always increases desired properties

misconceptions.statement: The compass needle is moved by the wind inside the casing.
misconceptions.why: Students look for a visible, mechanical cause for the movement of the needle.
misconceptions.fix: The compass casing is sealed; the needle moves due to the invisible magnetic field of the Earth.

probe.question: How does the needle move if the compass is inside a glass box?
probe.wrong_answer: Air currents inside the box push it.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Magnetism is the same thing as static electricity.
misconceptions.why: Both phenomena involve attraction and repulsion without physical contact.
misconceptions.fix: Magnetism is a property of certain materials like iron, while static electricity involves charges on surfaces.

probe.question: Will a magnet attract a plastic comb that has been rubbed on hair?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they both have attraction forces.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar effects must have the same cause
